title: Dielectrics
notes: Dielectrics are classified by their molecules. A non-polar molecule has no permanent dipole and acquires one by distortion in the field. A polar molecule already has a dipole and tends to line up with the field, against thermal jostling.
Either way, the field inside is the applied field minus the field of the bound surface charge. For a linear dielectric that fills the space, E = E_0 / K.
The bound charge is not free to flow in a wire. It stays on the dielectric surface. Leakage through a poor insulator is a separate, unwanted current.

The energy stored is Q^2/(2C) or (1/2) C V^2. These agree, but if you insert the dielectric at fixed Q, C rises and the energy falls. The difference is the work associated with pulling the dielectric in.
If you insert it at fixed V, C rises and the energy (1/2) C V^2 rises. The battery supplies that extra energy. Quoting the wrong case is a common exam error.
Above the dielectric strength the insulator breaks down and conducts. The working voltage must stay below that field times the thickness.
confusion: ❌ 'Dielectric constant is same as permittivity' ✅ Dielectric constant (relative permittivity) is a ratio (dimensionless), while permittivity has specific units (F/m).
❌ 'Dielectrics conduct electricity like metals' ✅ Dielectrics are insulators; they polarize in an electric field but do not conduct free charges like conductors.

❌ 'Polarization reduces the internal electric field' ✅ Polarization *creates* an opposing field, which results in a *net* reduction of the internal electric field compared to the external applied field.
Polar and non-polar both reduce the net field.
Bound charge does not flow around the circuit.
Energy falls at fixed Q and rises at fixed V.
E = E_0/K, not E_0 times K.
